sections.h2: What must a New Jersey seller disclose?
sections.html:
A New Jersey seller of a home must complete a property condition disclosure statement, known as the PCDS, and it must be signed. The form comes from the Division of Consumer Affairs under N.J.A.C. 13:45A-29.1(d), and the statute behind it is N.J.S.A. 56:8-19.1. P.L. 2024, c.32 made it a duty for real estate brokerage firms to obtain the signed statement from a residential seller.

A seller without an agent has the same job. The law says that a seller who is not working with a brokerage firm, or who works with a firm acting as transaction broker, must hand the statement to the buyer before the buyer becomes obligated under any contract. That timing matters. A statement delivered after the contract is signed does not meet the rule as written in section 2(e) of P.L. 2024, c.32.

sections.h2: Does New Jersey require a flood disclosure?
sections.html:
Yes. Since March 20, 2024, every seller of real property in the state must disclose flood risk information through the PCDS before the buyer is bound by a purchase contract. The Department of Environmental Protection explains two parts. The seller states whether the property is in FEMA's Special Flood Hazard Area or Moderate Flood Hazard Area, and the seller reports any actual knowledge about the property's flood risks.

The law is P.L. 2023, c.94, enacted July 3, 2023. The same page notes that sea-level rise is expected to meet or exceed 2.1 feet above 2000 levels by 2050 and that heavier rainfall raises flash flood risk inland. DEP offers a Flood Risk Notification Tool to help sellers find the zone answers. Because the duty applies to every seller, a cash sale or an as-is sale does not remove the question.

sections.h2: Which other New Jersey disclosures show up when you sell a house?
sections.html:
The Department of Banking and Insurance publishes a consumer guide that lists the items beyond the statement. Several belong to the seller, and others are mostly for the buyer to investigate.

  • Lead paint: for a house built before 1978, the seller must disclose known lead-based paint and hazards, give the buyer a lead disclosure form, and share any records or reports.
  • Material physical conditions: P.L. 2024, c.32 requires the listing brokerage to disclose existing material information about the property's physical condition that it knows or that a reasonable effort would reveal.
  • Stigmatized property: a seller and agent do not have to volunteer a haunting or a violent death, but must answer truthfully if the buyer asks.
  • Off-site conditions: municipal clerks keep lists of nearby conditions that may affect value, and buyers can review them.
  • Megan's Law: the county prosecutor decides how notice is given about convicted offenders in an area.

Mold, radon and asbestos appear in the same guide as inspection topics for the buyer, so expect questions about them during an inspection even though they are not separate seller forms.

sections.h2: What changed when P.L. 2024, c.32 took effect?
sections.html:
The law was signed July 10, 2024 and became effective August 1, 2024. The Real Estate Commission's Bulletin 24-11 explains that it adds designated agency as a fifth business relationship and requires a written brokerage services agreement in residential deals. Compensation terms in that agreement must say expressly that broker pay is negotiable and not set by law.

The Act also requires a posted sign at residential open houses warning visitors that the agent represents the seller and that information given to the agent is not confidential. A seller who lists with an agent should expect to sign the agency disclosure at the start and to hand over the PCDS soon after.

sections.h2: When can a New Jersey buyer or seller walk away after signing?
sections.html:
The Banking and Insurance guide describes an attorney review clause. When a licensee prepares the contract of sale, it must give buyer and seller three business days from delivery of the fully signed contract to consult an attorney. In that period the attorney can propose revisions or cancel the contract. If you hired an attorney to draft the contract instead, the guide says the review period may or may not be included, so ask the attorney.

This is where disclosure answers get tested. A statement that mentions flooding, a past repair or a lead history can lead the buyer's lawyer to ask for a repair credit or a price change during the review days. Answering fully at the start keeps those three days from becoming a renegotiation of surprises.

sections.h2: What happens after the buyer's inspection in New Jersey?
sections.html:
The state's buyer guide recommends an independent home inspection soon after a contract becomes binding, with the buyer present. The inspector reports on the structure, construction and mechanical systems and flags defects or items to replace. If the report shows problems, buyer and seller are held to the time limits written in the contract for delivering the report and for the seller to decide whether to correct the items.

For a seller, the practical point is to read those inspection and response deadlines before signing. Missing the contract's response window can leave you without a say in how a repair issue gets resolved. The guide tells buyers to consult an agent or attorney for the specifics of their contract, and sellers can do the same.

sections.h2: What seller taxes and forms come at a New Jersey closing?
sections.html:
The seller pays the Realty Transfer Fee when the deed is recorded. The Division of Taxation calculates it from the consideration in the deed, using a rate per $500 that rises with price. For a deal of $350,000 or less, the rate is $2.00 per $500 on the first $150,000, $3.35 from $150,000 to $200,000 and $3.90 from $200,000 to $350,000. An Affidavit of Consideration, Form RTF-1, claims any exemption. Sales above $1,000,000 also carry a graduated percent fee that starts at 1 percent of consideration.

A GIT/REP form is also recorded with the deed. New Jersey resident individuals, estates and trusts sign the GIT/REP-3. A nonresident seller prepays estimated gross income tax unless an assurance on that form applies, and the payment cannot be less than 2 percent of the total consideration in the deed. Executors and trustees complete the form for the estate or trust.

sections.h2: Can a seller in foreclosure still sell the house?
sections.html:
Yes. The NJ Courts say the Notice of Intent to Foreclose must state that the debtor can sell or transfer the title. After a sheriff sale the owner also has 10 days to redeem by buying back or selling. Disclosure rules still apply to a distressed sale, so the PCDS, flood answers and any lead form go to the buyer the same way.

The Judiciary also warns about foreclosure rescue and loan modification scams and recommends a free HUD and NJHMFA certified housing counselor. Anyone who asks for an upfront fee to save a home deserves a second look before you sign.

faqs.q: Is the property condition disclosure statement required for every New Jersey home sale?
faqs.a: For residential sales, yes. A licensee must obtain the signed statement from the seller, and a seller without an agent must give it to the buyer before the buyer is bound by the contract.

faqs.q: Do I have to disclose that my New Jersey house floods?
faqs.a: Yes, to the extent you know. Every seller must state whether the property is in a FEMA Special or Moderate Flood Hazard Area and report actual knowledge of flood risk before the buyer is obligated.

faqs.q: Is lead paint disclosure required in New Jersey?
faqs.a: Yes for houses built before 1978. The seller discloses known lead-based paint and hazards, provides the lead disclosure form and passes along any records or reports in hand.

faqs.q: Must a New Jersey seller disclose a death in the house?
faqs.a: Not unless asked. Stigmatized property, such as a violent death, does not have to be volunteered, but a seller or agent who knows the answer must give it truthfully when a buyer asks.

faqs.q: Who pays the realty transfer fee in New Jersey?
faqs.a: The seller pays it. The Division of Taxation sets rates per $500 of consideration, and the fee is collected when the deed is recorded with the county clerk.
